 Prosecutors in Naresh Bhatt’s murder trial say surveillance video shows him dumping trash during wife’s disappearance
 By Linh Bui 
 October 21, 2026 | 
 9:26 PM 
 | 
 Testimony continued Wednesday in the murder trial of Naresh Bhatt, the Manassas Park, Virginia, man accused of killing and dismembering his wife. Mamta Kafle Bhatt was last heard from on July 29, 2024, and her body was never found.
 Prosecutors first focused on surveillance video showing Naresh Bhatt wearing gloves and dumping trash around the time of his wife’s disappearance. Gabriela Manzanares, the property manager at Fairfield Crossing Apartments in Falls Church, said Bhatt leased an apartment there. She was unaware he had a home in Manassas Park.

 Manzanares testified that surveillance video from July 31, 2024, showed Bhatt throwing bags into the trash compactor.
 “He’s carrying it as if the bag were to break, as if it were something heavy,” she said. “He is cradling the bag with one arm and holding it upright with his right hand.”
 Prosecutors then questioned Brahayan Ramirez Pena, who rented the couple’s basement and lived in their Manassas Park home on Heather Court for about two years. He testified that before police officers arrived on Aug. 2, 2024, for a welfare check, Naresh Bhatt had asked him to help rearrange furniture. Ramirez Pena said he helped move the bed, nightstand and dresser in the master bedroom.
 While being cross-examined, Ramirez Pena said he never witnessed the couple argue or fight. He said he didn’t realize Mamta Kafle Bhatt was missing until talking to officers.
 Jose Barajas Ayala also took the stand. He has a gardening business that includes landscaping, tree removal, and construction. On Aug. 1, 2024, he was working at a neighboring home on Heather Court when Naresh Bhatt inquired about cutting his grass. Barajas Ayala agreed to come twice a month and charge $40 each time.
 “I saw the guy [Naresh Bhatt] come out and he was trying to cut a small tree trunk with a saw. And I saw that he was doing it in an erratic fashion,” Barajas Ayala said through an interpreter.
 He said he demonstrated how to properly use the green Ryobi saw. Then Naresh Bhatt offered him the saw, along with batteries and a charger, in exchange for the day’s work.
 When Barajas Ayala returned to the property on Aug. 28, 2024, to cut the grass, a neighbor informed him about Naresh Bhatt’s arrest and showed him a news story. He debated what to do with the saw with his co-workers, and ultimately brought it to the Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office on Sept. 9. He was asked directly if he saw anyone “use the saw to chop up a human body” and said no.
 Senior Deputy Thomas Wheeler with the Spotsylvania County Sheriff’s Office was a detective with the Manassas Police Department when he was assigned to investigate Mamta Kafle Bhatt’s missing persons case. He testified that on Aug. 15, 2024, he spoke to Naresh Bhatt at his home.
 “He previously stated they had had arguments. He stated that most of those arguments were from things outside of the marriage,” Wheeler said. “They argued about his parents being there at their address. That she, Mamta, did not want his parents at the address, and wanted them to go back, and he wanted them to stay because they were helping out.”
 His body-camera footage was introduced, showing Bhatt recalling the days around his wife’s disappearance.
 The judge asked the prosecution to be more efficient and streamline testimony moving forward to give the defense and jury deliberations sufficient time, noting courts are closed on Election Day and Veterans Day.
 Bhatt was arrested in August 2024. He is charged with first-degree murder among other charges in his wife’s death.
 The jury consists of six men and 11 women, including the five alternates.

 Voting-related measures on November ballots include a voter ID push targeting mail-in ballots
 By The Associated Press 
 October 22, 2026 | 
 6:07 AM 
 | 
 Advocates for greater voter identification requirements are pursuing a new approach in some states: a mandate to place driver's license or partial Social Security numbers on mail-in ballots. 
Variations of the voter ID proposals are being decided in the midterm elections in California, Colorado and Nevada — three states where conservative activists collected petition signatures to bypass Democratic-led legislatures and place the issue directly before voters.
The voter ID measures are among about 30 questions on November ballots affecting state policies on voting and elections. They account for roughly 1 in 5 of all state ballot measures nationwide. Some mirror policies that President Donald Trump has pushed unsuccessfully at the national level and build off a Republican narrative that noncitizen voting is a problem, though data indicates it is rare. 
Several measures address changes to congressional voting districts, as part of a national redistricting battle spurred by Trump. Others could change the way primaries are conducted, make it more difficult for voters to amend their state constitutions or — in Missouri — make it harder for lawmakers to change measures that voters approve.
